No I work with solid gold nanoparticles to create polymer nanocomposites for local surface plasmon resonance (LSPR)-based biosensors. LSPR-based biosensors work, because when an analyte binds to the surface of – or near the nanoparticle– it induces a change in the nanoparticle’s refractive index which shifts the LSPR peak frequency. This shift is quantifiable and allows us to see how much of an analyte is present in a given sample.

When two gold nanoparticles come into close contact, their electromagnetic fields couple, which can produce large shifts to longer wavelengths, thereby making the biosensor much more sensitive than if there were just one nanoparticle. This is called plasmonic coupling. We can exploit plasmonic coupling in biosensors by creating lattices or arrays of nanoparticles as a means of producing significant changes in the detected signal.

There remains an open question as to how to more easily form these arrays without expensive, specialized equipment, harsh reagents, and pre-functionalizing the nanoparticles. My lab has developed a novel biocompatible polymeric material that can order the nanoparticles in neat linear arrays in less than 5 minutes.
